sentences.text: The plan for the extension came to the town in the February and it was, everybody agreed, a good plan.
The harbour needed it.

The wall of 1961 was built for wooden boats and the fishing fleet was gone; what came in now were ferries in the summer and yachts, and both wanted deeper water and a longer arm, and there was money from the region for exactly this and the money had a date on it.
The proposal took the arm out a further hundred and forty metres and turned it about fifteen degrees south.

Ela's father had the drawing on the table for a week and was in favour, and so was almost everybody, and Ela would like that stated clearly because the story is not about a town resisting a development.
The town wanted it.
Her own family wanted it.
Two of her cousins had left for Athens in the previous four years and the ferry berth was the only argument anybody had for them coming back.
The consultation was held in the school hall in March and Ela went with her grandmother because her grandmother went to everything.
The engineer was a woman from Patras called Despina Vlachou and Ela would like it on the record that she was excellent.
She had drawings.
She answered every question, including four that were rude.

When the man from the hardware shop asked about the sand she did not brush him off; she put up a slide with three years of survey data and explained longshore drift for six minutes to a room of eighty people, most of whom had known about longshore drift their entire lives without having a word for it.

And then somebody at the back said: "What about the turtles?" And Despina Vlachou said that this had been considered, and put up the environmental assessment, and it was a real assessment and it was not a box-ticking exercise.
The nesting beach was protected.
The works were outside the season.
There was a monitoring condition.
She said that the assessment showed no nesting within the affected zone.
There was a particular quality of silence in that hall which Ela has thought about a great many times since, because at twelve she could feel it and could not read it.
About eighty people knew something and not one of them stood up.
Ela looked round the hall.
She saw the man from the hardware shop, who is in the 1961 photograph, look at the floor.
She saw her grandmother's hands on the back of the chair in front of her.
She saw two women from the church turn very slightly towards each other and not say anything.
Then the meeting moved on to parking, and the parking took forty minutes.
